utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic and Vladimir Santic also know as "Vlado".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Our first witness this morning is witness number 1 on the list that we have established for this week. This witness will testify under a number of protective measures. We are now quite used to them. Pseudonym Z will be attributed to this witness today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Very well. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Witness Z.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Will you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document is Exhibit 243.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Good morning, witness. First of all, I would like to inform you of the fact that this Chamber has granted you a number of protective measures. Your face will be distorted on the public screens and you have been attributed a pseudonym. Therefore, you can testify without fearing that anything you will say will be known publicly, and you can say everything you have been a witness to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: In 1992/1993, did you live in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Without giving too precise information, could you tell us where in Ahmici you used to live, which area of the village? Without showing us the location of your house, could you show us the general area in which you lived in Ahmici, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This region (indicating). Just a moment, please. I apologise. Just a moment. I'm a little nervous.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please take your time. Take the time to orientate yourself on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you now please describe your family, and could you tell us who were the members of your family in 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived with my father and mother. I was married at the time, I had a wife. My father was born in 1946, my mother was born in 1950. My wife was born in 1973. We lived happily. We didn't have any problems. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Where do you live today, Witness Z?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today I live in Ahmici. I went back home there. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) entered the village officially, and we started to rebuild our houses and clear up the village, and up till about 10 to 15 days ago when my house was completed and I went back to my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you've only went back to Ahmici very recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you a number of things on the period of time going from '92 to March 1993. At that time what was your job? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was a member of the Territorial Defence, I spent most of my time in Vitez, from October -- the 20th of October I was in the village of Ahmici. I came there on assignment as member of the Territorial Defence, and I spent most of my time at the headquarters of the Territorial Defence. In October 1992, I spent that time in Ahmici, up until the day when the first conflict took place. I was in Ahmici for 15 days before that, because I didn't go to Vitez. So I spent those 15 days, that period, in Ahmici, until the relevant authorities decided on a conflict. I was not able to take up my duties because the conflict was ongoing. And as members of the Territorial Defence, and generally as the Muslim Bosnian population, we were not allowed to move about, so that I did not go to my own house because of that in 1992, the 20th of October, as I say, up until the 35th (sic). I was not able to go back home. I was in the upper part of Ahmici. That is the 30th of May. But once, on the eighth or ninth day, when the relevant authorities at a high level, I don't know exactly, but they decided -- we decided to be at the entrance to Ahmici as a sort of checkpoint, because the Croats held that point and did not allow anybody to enter the village after that decision was made. And as I lived in Lower Ahmici, I was assigned to that particular point. It only lasted perhaps one shift, and it lasted for two hours, not more. That was the shift that I worked. And that was the first time that I went home to see what was happening, whether it had been looted. Generally speaking, nothing had been taken away but the house was shelled. And my mother and my father, on the 20th, that is to say the night between the 19th and the 20th of October, they were in the house with some other villagers and those that had survived the shelling of the house. They were in the house. And it was only on the 20th, at about noon, that they left the house and went towards Upper Ahmici. And on that occasion, I was at that checkpoint where I was -- the point to which I was assigned to do a two-hour shift, and I can tell you the names of the people who were with me if you like, because there were others with me. There was Mirjan Kupreskic, Ivica Kupreskic, Vinko Vidovic and myself. And that is when I saw them for the first time after the conflict. We were all together at the entrance to the village. And then after 15 -- 15 days later, for the first time, I went -- as we were lodged in Vitez, in the secondary school centre in Vitez called Boris Kidric centre, and as the conflict had already broken out and they were all expelled and had fled to Stari Vitez. So that it was only after 15 days that I went to the Territorial Defence headquarters to report for duty there. As I was in the Military Police, I was in charge of the security of the Territorial Defence headquarters. And I also went up to the frontline, towards the Serbs, frequently, towards Vlasic, towards Visoko, and we were escorted by the army and so on. Right up until the conflict in 1993, I was on the duty at the Territorial Defence headquarters in Stari Vitez, and I went home from time to time. Sometimes I would stay 15 days, depending what the duties were and what my job was. On the 16th of April, that terrible day of 1993, that fateful day, I had come back one or two days prior to that. I had gone home prior to that date to have a rest, and that is how I found myself there on -- in my house on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: A moment ago you told us about this checkpoint that was established at the entrance of Ahmici after the events of 1992. What was the aim of this checkpoint? Why was it established there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, one or two days before, that is to say on the 19th or 20th, I had come back home, and as the situation was not as it should have been, there were conflicts in Busovaca, that's when they attacked Stani (phoen), Merdani and Kovacevci, we saw this, because it's not far away from where we are. There was fire, everything was burning. I can say something I forgot to mention a moment ago, and that is that when Eso Salkic was killed, that is when he was blown to smithereens in his house, he lived in Nadioci, and we went to the funeral, to the Genaza as it's called, and I saw a VBR, a grenade launcher, in the Vlasko Polje, and it was targeted toward Merdani, in that direction. And when we went to the funeral, we saw that it had been positioned in that way. It has nine grenades. It's a small rocket-propelled grenade launcher. At the control checkpoint we were issued a sort of order, I don't know by whom the order was given, but we were told to leave the checkpoint on the 19th of October. As I was already working in the Military Police, and as I had already been at the combined checkpoints, I was designated to man that checkpoint, because on the 19th, in Vitez, the municipality of Vitez, they had started to confiscate cars, vehicles. They looted flats and stormed into houses but we knew nothing of this. We learned of these incidents later on. We learnt of everything that had happened on the 19th. And, as I say, the situation was very tense. Armies passed, all kinds of armies. There were all kinds of uniforms passing by. I succeeded in coming. I was able to come. Otherwise, they did not allow us -- that is to say, our side in the Territorial Defence, they didn't allow us to go home for our own safety, so as not to be beaten up, for example, because that's what they did do. I was not able to carry a rifle anywhere, only if I hid it somewhere in my car and was able to bring it into my house, secretly. But generally, it stayed at the Territorial Defence headquarters. So I was at the checkpoint up until approximately 3.00 in the morning. I went home. I went home to sleep, because I was very tired. It was late. I woke up at about half past four. I was very nervous. We were all nervous and tense. I got up. My mother stayed in the house. She was the only one that stayed there. I went towards the upper part of the village of Ahmici. We call that part --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you Witness Z, but I have a question I want to put to you. You spoke of three individuals a moment ago, three individuals who were present at the checkpoint which was established after October 1992. It was established at the entrance of Ahmici. You gave us the three names of these individuals, but could you tell us how these people were dressed when you saw them, and could you also tell us if they were carrying weapons or guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came there, I found Mirjan Kupreskic there, as well as Ivica Kupreskic and Vinko Vidovic. All three were wearing uniforms. They had automatic rifles. They had camouflage uniforms. They did not have any caps on their heads. They had uniforms and rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you have Croat neighbours close to your house or close to your parents' house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not far off from me, not even 100 metres away, my next door neighbour was Vlado Santic. His father was also there, Jozo Santic. And not far off from him there was Drago Josipovic. That is my immediate circle of neighbours, not 100 metres off from us, because I am from that lower part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us more about Vlado Santic? What kind of relationship did you have with this individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, good. We had good relationships. Even to the present day, I say hello to him after everything that we have experienced and lived through. I have nothing to say to him. He's a good neighbour. He's okay. His father and his brother, they're okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And what was your relationship like with your other neighbour, Drago Josipovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Josipovic. Well, I say hello when he says hello. He wasn't a good neighbour though. Can I give an example to the Court, illustrating what kind of man Drago Josipovic was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in 1992, we organised ourselves in the village to have a collection for the hospital in Travnik, sort of a humanitarian aid, a collection drive, as there was a crisis everywhere with the conflicts just beginning at Vlasic, and the country was in the process of disintegrating. We, as the villagers, myself and my mother, for the lower part of the village, and the others were up in the upper part, in Upper Ahmici. We wanted to make a collection drive for the hospital in Travnik. Some of the women would make pies. We would collect milk for the hospital in Travnik. We took this relief -- or it came to the house of Luca, who is Drago's mother. Drago Josipovic was sitting at the table with another man whom I did not know, and we arrived at the house and we started explaining why we had come and what we were doing, that we were collecting food for the hospital in Travnik. And he said angrily at that, "Why are you doing this? It's not your job to collect food, we have our own." And his mother Luca said to him, angrily, she liked to swear a bit when she spoke, and she said, "Well, begging your pardon, don't shit around. He's -- she's come to me and not to you." So the mother brought to the school in Ahmici, her contribution, which is where we were collecting food and which we took to Travnik to the hospital by combi. As I say, we would say hello to one another when we saw each other, but we did not have any good relations and we did not go visiting each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you know Drago Josipovic's wife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Slavica. And that is -- how shall I put it? Well, she comes from an angry Ustashe family. That's what her brother was, Nenad, and I suppose some of it rubbed off on her as well. It seems to be in their blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What is the name of the brother of Drago Josipovic's wife? You said Nenad, I think, but what is his family name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Drago Josipovic dressed in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did see him previously, and he was assigned to this area where we used to collect. He was at my entrance, and whenever the situation was not as it should have been, he was there with a rifle, usually wearing civilian clothes, but I did see him in uniform, as well, on occasion. He would always move around. He always knew what was happening. He was well-informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can we then say that all the Croats in Ahmici, at that particular point in time, were dressed with a uniform and carried a gun around? Was that something that was customary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not everybody wore uniforms, because some people worked in the firm, others at checkpoints. Depending on what assignment you were given, that is the type of clothing you would wear. If somebody was in the Croatian Defence Council, and they were all in the Croatian Defence Council, in fact, but, for the most part, the uniforms were kept hidden at home. Some of them did wear uniforms all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You mentioned a moment ago your Croat neighbour, Vlado Santic. Did you ever see him wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He did not wear a uniform. He avoided doing so. On one occasion, he said, "If the Muslims were to patrol the village and take up watches, so will I. If they are not going to do it, then I won't either." I think that he was forced to put on a uniform, which, allegedly -- on Tuesday in 1993, on Tuesday, three days before that, he went to Turbe, up to the frontline. I think that that is the first occasion where he wore his uniform. He didn't want to put a uniform on and to move about. He wanted to be like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would just like to specify that the Vlado Santic that the witness is telling us about is not the accused. It's an individual who has the very same name as the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can you tell us more about Dragan Papic? Did you have any particular kind of relationship with that man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were neighbours. We had a good relationship. His father would come to our house, too. We would visit. You know, we weren't on bad terms. But what got into Dragan Papic and all these others and into the people in general, what kind of hatred this was, as of late, I mean, when this first conflict broke out and the second conflict broke out, ever since then, we haven't had any contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dragan Papic wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He wore a black uniform non-stop. The sleeves were a bit too short for him. He always wore a uniform. From October 1992 and then until 1993, he was invariably seen in a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did he carry a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On one occasion, I saw him carrying a sniper towards Vlatko Kupreskic's. He went in that direction, towards them, and he went through the village by the school, and that is where we saw each other, as we passed each other by the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did you have a gun and did you use and carry a gun in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had an automatic rifle which I brought from Slimena. It was a burned rifle because we had really improvised the rifle butt and things like that. It was not a safe rifle. It was a rifle, but it was not 100 per cent safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Could you tell us where this weapon came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's from the former Yugoslav People's Army, from their warehouse in Slimena, which belonged to Travnik. It was taken over, handed over, whatever, this warehouse, because it had been mined, too. We got all of this out of the debris. There were some new rifles, some real rifles, but the Croatian army had taken some of it, the Territorial Defence, the HVO, the people themselves got some things out, and that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, I would like you now to tell us about the events which took place in April 1993. First of all, would you please tell us what you did on the night from the 15th to the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, the silence was unbearable. One cannot describe it, this atmosphere, the way it was, as if there were no birds around. You could only hear a car or two pass by. In the evenings when I was off, we would go out in front of the house, and that is where I went that evening, too. I was there until 2.00 a.m. with a refugee, Galib Imsirevic, who lived in my uncle's house. He was a refugee from Karaula. He and I were there. We were taking care of the house, walking around. The atmosphere wasn't that great, really. We were all tense. We were all nervous. We were all afraid as to what would happen, what would not happen, whether there would be a war, whether there would not be a war. No one trusted anyone anymore, but we took care of each, and we tried to make sure that nobody walked up to the house. I was there until 2.00 with Galib Imsirevic. After 2.00, his father came, and he said, "Why don't you go into the house now and I'll stay on for awhile? I'll take care of it." They were there with their family, wife and children. I didn't have any family then, but my mother was in the house. My father wasn't there. He was a driver. He worked in the Princip factory, and he was away on business in Croatia. At 2.00, he took over and we went into the house, and I went to bed in a uniform. I just laid down. All of a sudden, I heard shooting. This was the morning of the 16th. Believe me, I didn't know where I was when I heard this shooting. It was nearby. It was really nearby. When I got out of my room into the hallway, I saw my mother standing there. She was lost. The first bullet had hit the niche through the window in the kitchen where my mother was asleep. She got up and she was beside herself. She didn't know what was going on because she had been asleep to, and she didn't know what was going on. I was just telling her to duck, to lie down on the floor, so that they wouldn't start shooting at the windows again; otherwise, they would hit her. Well, that's how it started, this second conflict of the 16th of April. I was at home until 8.00, around 8.00. I was at home with my mother and my wife. In the morning when the shooting broke out, I opened the door. Because I ran to the door with a rifle in my hand, and I saw people in uniform running to my yard. They had helmets on, too. They were running from my house towards my uncle's house, up there, towards the road. I saw at least ten men there. I didn't recognise them, but they were running across there. There was some construction material there for building a new house, so they were running that way. I didn't know at all what was going on in my uncle's house. The house was drilled, his house and mine. In the morning, I would peek out of the window from the corner every now and then, and I saw, at that moment, I don't know, it seemed to me like five minutes or ten minutes, Abdulah Ahmic's and Fahran Ahmic's houses were on fire. I saw bullets from anti-aircraft guns. You could see this part called Krcevine, that is, the lower part of Ahmici, near the lower mosque and the school. So it was at these houses that the shooting was aimed against. I realised that these houses were on fire, too, and I had the feeling, at that time, that within five or ten minutes, as I was telling you, a house would burn down, because a lot of wood was on these houses, not only the roofs, but beams. We didn't know what to do, whether to go some place. If I had any possibility of defending myself, I would have, but I didn't have any possibility of doing that. My mother was there and my wife, who was pregnant at the time, was there. She had already had a baby out of fear. It was a stillborn baby, and she had to hide all day with my mother and these refugees. So, of course, she suffered the consequence of having a stillborn baby.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, on that particular morning, did you use your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I was afraid for my wife's safety and my mother's safety. Were I on my own, perhaps I would have defended myself, because I think it was my duty. I mean, what were these men in uniform with rifles doing in my yard anyway? What would they be doing there, otherwise? Why would they come, except to kill me? If I were on my own, I would have defended myself. But had I been shooting, myself, then they could have killed my wife or my mother or whoever. It was all the same to me whether they would kill me, but I didn't want them to kill my wife or my mother, not to harm them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What did you do with your weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw men in uniform in my yard, I took off my uniform, the uniform I had. I hid my rifle in the oven. It's a Rayburn type oven, stove. I took off the magazine clip, too. I had that also. I put all of that into the stove, and I had trousers and a jacket on and a T-shirt, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you please hand this blow-up to the witness? Your Honour, maybe we could go into a closed session. This would enable the witness to tell us where his house was located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. Let us go into closed session. (Closed session) 25 (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, could you show us on this photograph the point on the road where the UNPROFOR vehicle stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From Vlado's we ran here, here. This is where we ran out. This is where one APC stopped, and the other one turned here (indicating). This one turned here by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Using a marker, could you please put an indication on the point where the vehicle stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two APCs. The first turned at this point, and the second turned here (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's fine. Mr. Usher, could you please hand this photograph over to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 245.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, could you please tell us what this photograph depicts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That is the scene when we had come up in front of the APCs. This is my mother. It was a group of us. I can't tell you exactly who is who there on the picture, although I know exactly who was there. I can just recognise my mother. When the APC turned round, it turned round in front of us in the direction of Vitez, as if to go back. At that point the first APC came back, and the doors opened and we started going in. The group of civilians started entering the APC. At that moment, on the right-hand side, I had probably -- was the fifth to go in or the sixth. One group went up to this APC, and the rest of us, eight of us, there were eight of us in the first carrier, and at that time, on the right-hand side, I saw Aladin who was working there waved to me, but I wasn't able to help him because I was afraid myself. I was afraid of being killed, because at that time I don't think that they had any idea that an IFOR or a SFOR would turn up. So we were all frightened. I saw him on the right-hand side, to the right of me, but we were busy getting into the APC as fast as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So this photograph was taken when the UNPROFOR vehicle started turning around and before you went in to leave Ahmici. You told us about this individual who signalled to you, an individual named Aladin. Do you know the family name of this individual, and also, could you tell us where he was exactly and why was he signalling to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aladin Karahodza, Karahodza was his surname, and he worked at the Veternica fuel stock as a night watchman. I didn't know what had happened to him. On the 15th, at night, he was on duty doing his shift, between the 15th and the 16th, at the Ogrjev plant where he was a night watchman. He waved to me, and it was only on the next day that I learned that he had been captured, and that -- on the 16th, in the morning, Drago Josipovic came to him and took his official gun away from him and told him -- and threatened him, and he was in the room the whole day, and I am very sorry that he is not alive here with me today to confirm and bear out what I am saying. He waved to us for us to help him, but we weren't able to help him because we were frightened ourselves. I didn't know that he had gone outside. I only learned of this the next day, because as I say, we were going to the Travnik hospital, and I was in shock, and I woke up at the hospital in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: This individual is dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the 17th --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to make an objection. The question is hearsay. That is to say what somebody else told the witness. All the more so as the witness, Mr. President, has, on several occasions so far with regard to the circumstances, given different statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, but you know, we do admit hearsay evidence under our Rules of Procedure, so it is not to be ruled out. So you can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: So you stepped into the UNPROFOR APC. At that precise moment in time did you notice anything else around you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went in I saw Aladin on the right-hand side waving to us. At that moment it was my turn to go into the vehicle, and I looked to the left where I saw a group of soldiers led by -- I saw Drago Josipovic with four other men, four other soldiers who were with him, and they were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: How far was this group of soldiers from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't far away. Twenty metres away, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the entrance, the gate towards Hasim and his son Fahran Ahmic, and he stood at the entrance, at the gateway by the fence. They were just standing there, and I was able to recognise him because he was not standing far off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: You told us he was wearing a uniform. What kind of uniform was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were the camouflage type of uniform, dark green with lighter green patches. A pattern of light and dark green.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Did he carry a gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did have rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: What kind of weapon was he carrying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he had an automatic rifle usually, and on that occasion he had the automatic rifle. Whether it was the one he always carried or another one, I don't know, but it was an automatic rifle, and he was standing at -- first at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: And, for instance, did you notice if he was wearing some camouflage paint on his face or another kind of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, his face was clean. He didn't have anything painted on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, please take another look at the blow-up of the map and please show us, as precisely as possible, where Drago Josipovic stood when you noticed him. Witness Z. Witness Z, on this photograph, the one that is on the desk.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we were here the APC was here, and that is the entrance to the house (indicating). This is Hasim Ahmic's house, and his son Fahran. It was here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, with an arrow, could you show us the place where Drago Josipovic stood when you noticed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here (indicating). There (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The usher will now give you another photograph. Mr. Usher, could you hand this photograph over to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 246.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, what can we see on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph shows Drago Josipovic's house. This is where the APCs turned around and where we stood. This fence wasn't here at the time. You can see Fahran's house. This is Drago Josipovic's house. We went into the APC here, but the fence wasn't there (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Can we see on this photograph, the place where Drago Josipovic stood when you went into the APCs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you can't see it on the photograph. It would be this way, but you can't see it on the photograph (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: With an arrow, could you indicate the place where you stepped into the APC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was here (marks).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I will now give you a third and last photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number 247.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, what can we see on this picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the upper part of Ogrjev which is where Aladin Karahodza worked. He was a night watchman here. That's the entrance to the plant. I saw Aladin Karahodza waving from this point, to save him, I suppose. I saw him here (indicating), and that is the Ogrjev plant belonging to Veternica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: On the big photograph, could you show us where this particular structure is located? On the map behind you, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's where it was (indicating). That is the Ogrjev facility. That is the Veternica Ogrjev facility, and it was here to my right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: For the record, the witness is showing a facility lying next to the road going from Vitez to Busovaca. It is at about the same height as Drago Josipovic's house but on the other side of the road. Is that right witness, Z?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness. I would only like to tender Exhibits numbers 243 to 247. Exhibits 243 and 244 should be tendered under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier, could you please just have the witness indicate on the aerial photograph where Drago Josipovic's house is? I don't think we have it from that. You said it's opposite the Ogrjev facility, but I'm not quite sure where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, the witness did not indicate that particular house.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, could you show us where Drago Josipovic's house is on that particular photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The house of Drago Josipovic is located here, opposite the Ogrjev facility (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Witness Z, using the green marker, for example -- green, please. So using the green marker, could you please put a cross on this particular house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. (Marks). That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. I think it's better for the Defence counsel if we take a break now, 30-minute break, so when we come back you can tell us who is going to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Your Honours. The witness will be questioned by Defence Counsel Luka Susak, Petar Puliselic, Jadranka Slokovic-Glumac, and Ranko Radovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Susak?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Witness Z, my name is Counsel Luka Susak, and I'm going to ask you a few questions. Will you tell us how many times you made statements before coming to the Court here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: No. You made three statements. Let me remind you. You gave a statement for the first time on the 16th and 17th of November, 1997; the second was given on the 2nd of February, 1998; the third on the 10th of May, 1998. You stated that you were in the house of Drago Josipovic, if I understood you correctly, when you sought humanitarian aid for the hospital in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went to his mother's house, which is his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that that was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Will you tell us when that was, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, perhaps, June or July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: June or July 1992, you say. Since when were you in the police, in the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: The Military Police, since when were you a member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the Military Police when it separated, when the Croatian Defence Council was started up and the Croats, who were with us, they separated. We went to join the Territorial Defence, the Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Let me remind you, this was on the 6th of April, 1992, that is, what you said in your first statement, at least.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How come that, as a policeman, you went from house to house and, in concrete terms, to Drago Josipovic's house to ask for humanitarian aid, because it is not usual, customary, for the police to go visiting houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was wearing a civilian uniform. I was not in uniform. It was my free time. I went with my mother to keep her company, so as not to let her go alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Let me remind you of the law on criminal proceedings and the penal code, which was in force at the time, whereby a military policeman or an ordinary policeman is a person of authority, even when not wearing a police uniform. All the more so -- just a moment, please. All the more so that in the surrounding villages and in the village itself, people knew that you were a policeman. But never mind, I'm not going to go into that matter anymore. Was your father a member of the Territorial Defence or was he in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a member of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did he have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What kind of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a PAP, a semi-automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was it okay? Did it function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was issued this when he went to defend civilians up at the frontline towards the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you tell us who was in the Territorial Defence headquarters in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Ahmici, well, I belonged to the Territorial Defence of Vitez. I don't know about Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that you went to Vlado Santic's shed. How long did you stay there before the APCs arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, from half past eight in the morning until four or half past four in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said 1630 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, half past four, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You were questioned by an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor on the 16th and 17th of November, 1997?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How come, on that occasion, you did not mention Karahodza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aladin. I said that I gave two statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'm talking about this particular one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me say to the Judges that I thought his name was Aladin Sehaganovic. Let me explain, please. I thought his name was Sehaganovic, that that was his surname, because he was married to a Sehaganovic. It was only later on that I learned that his surname was Karahodza.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Let me remind you that you did not mention this second individual when you were first interviewed. You never mentioned him. You didn't say he had a different name. How do you explain this, that you mentioned this second individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know I mentioned him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But you signed the statement, and there's no mention of him made in the statement, nevertheless, in front of the Bosnian police, who interrogated you one year later or, more precisely, on the 2nd of February, 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I explain, please? We did not have enough time when I was questioned for the second time -- not the second time, the first time. Just a moment, please. Let me explain. The first time I was questioned, I had not arrived at that point. We were interrupted, and then we continued later on. After a certain amount of time had elapsed, we went on with the second statement where I mention Aladin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You made your second statement, and it was a statement of less than half a page in length. I have the feeling that you were in a hurry here when the Bosnian police questioned you. How long were you questioned for by the Bosnian police? Who did you give the statement to on the 2nd of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I gave the statement in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: This statement is a little more than half a page in length. How long did it take you to make that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About two or three hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: In view of the fact that it is over half a page, it seems that it was related to the question of Aladin Karahodza. However, you made your first statement, and it was a six-page statement, in my translation, which means that it was an exhaustive statement. However, you failed to mention the individual?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It wasn't an exhaustive statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But you were questioned on the 16th and 17th of November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps we didn't complete it and we continued later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So this took two days and this was a comprehensive statement. How come you did not remember that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as I said, every village could write volumes and volumes about the events they experienced and everything that happened. You can't remember everything immediately, because there were a lot of events. A lot of things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that when you went up onto the road when the APCs arrived that you put on women's clothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In front of the shed of Vlado Santic, I put on a woman's skirt and a scarf and went across to the APC to stop anybody from recognising me, because I was the only military-abled man there. I was the only man among all the women there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that a female gave you these clothes to put on, if I heard you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was Fikreta. "Fikra" is what we called her, Imsirevic. She is Galib Imsirevic's mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Let me remind you that you gave a statement in Zenica, but you told the investigator that your mother had given you the clothing to wear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not my mother. This was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Then the investigator recorded this in an incorrect manner, and he did so over the two days that you gave your statement. When you entered the APC, who entered it first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember who went in to the carrier first. There were eight of us in the APC. I think that I went in fifth or sixth. I can't quite remember, and you can't ask me to remember the exact line and who went first and who went last. I don't recall this exactly. I didn't pay attention to who went into the APC first, because at that particular moment, I saw Aladin, and my attention was diverted towards Aladin, so that I failed to see who went into the APC first.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How did you see Aladin Karahodza?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I saw him standing over there in front of the little house by the Ogrjev facility, in front of the Ogrjev building. He was waving to us to help us, I suppose, because he couldn't go anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So he was in front of the little building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How come you said that Aladin told you that Drago Josipovic locked him up in the night watchman's house? Tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did give that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But today you say he was standing in front of the building, whereas, at the time, you said that he was locked in and that Drago Josipovic had locked him in the caretaker's building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he saw us and when the APC arrived and he saw us, there was, sort of, a glass partition, glass door, and he broke down the glass door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you say that he had broken down the glass door?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But today you said that he was standing in front of the building. This means that he broke down the glass and was able to get out. But beforehand, you said that he was locked up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the day after, on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that you were in shock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the APC, and when I entered the APC, and that was somewhere near Travnik, perhaps it was by Nova Bila or Dolac, I went into shock. I had some convulsions and went into shock. Whether from the fear or something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When did you regain consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I woke up in the hospital room, and I had a drip in my arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was about 10 to 15 minutes after being carried out of the APC into the hospital room. The drip woke me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How long were you in hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just spent the night in the hospital until the 17th, in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to a friend of mine's who was in Travnik where my wife and mother had spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When you went home, did you have a rest or did you go to the battlefront?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent 19 days in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But what about the 17th when you came to that house, what did you do when you came to the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, nothing. You know, it was a general state of shock, because I heard that people had been killed, and I spent 19 days in Travnik. I was not in the army at the time. I was nowhere. On the nineteenth day, I went to Zenica. I was transported with the wounded, the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: But if you were in shock on the 16th, what did you do on the 17th? Did you have a rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I rested in the house of my friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you spend the whole day in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you leave the house on the 17th at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I went out into the fresh air with my wife for a bit to have a rest from everything, because there was still a great deal of fear in my head, but we didn't move around too much because the Croatian Defence Council was in Travnik as well. So we weren't able to move around Travnik much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you met anybody in Travnik on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just (redacted)and those of us who had escaped and the wounded. I went to visit them in hospital the next day. I walked around a bit with my wife and then my mother came later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you, on that particular day, meet any of the members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did see some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, she was not a member of the army proper. It was a female,(redacted), and she was wounded in the leg. She was in the hospital, as well as Munir Ahmic and Ibrahim Karic, and Fahrudin Ahmic was also there. They were lying down in hospital. They were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Those are all the individuals who you met?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were all the people from Ahmici who were in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did any of them come to your house on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At my house, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that in Travnik, Karahodza told you of the events that had taken place. When did he tell you of these events, when you just told us that you didn't see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say I didn't see him. You didn't ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I asked you to enumerate the individuals, the male individuals, that came to your house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not meet him at the house or in town. We met in front of the hospital, in front of the Travnik Hospital, when I was visiting Munir and Fahrudin and (redacted) the little Karic boy. Then I saw him going out. I did not know that he was out until the 17th. I did not know that the UNPROFOR soldier had led him up to the APC and that he was taken to Travnik with me. I didn't know until I saw him on the 17th in the morning, sometime around 11.00 a.m., thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You seem to remember things when I tell you of the incidents, and then you seem to recall the events, but previously, you did not mention Karahodza. You said --

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. I object. I don't like the manner in which Mr. Susak is interrogating the witness. I object to this latest question. I do not agree. Mr. Susak asks of the witness which members of the army he met in Travnik. Witness Z does not mention a particular name that Mr. Susak is waiting for, and because the witness does not mention this particular name, he says that the witness is not coherent with himself. But I think Mr. Susak is laying a trap for the witness, and I don't think that's a proper way to go about cross-examining a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is sustained. I wonder whether Counsel Susak would be so kind as to put his questions in a different way and, in any case, to move on to other questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is difficult for me to accept this objection, because in the statement made on the 10th of May, '98, it says that on the 17th of April, Karahodza told this witness about this event. But then when I asked him, previously, which persons these were, he never mentioned Aladin Karahodza. Then he remembered, subsequently, so that is why I put this question to him because he says so in the statement. It's not that I made it up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that you saw Drago Josipovic with four other soldiers; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that he wore a uniform and that he had weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: What does that mean, that he had a uniform? Did he have a cap?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you explain what he looked like, what the characteristics of his appearance were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he was about 165 to 170 centimetres tall. He had a cap on his head, a multi-coloured cap, a chubby face with a big moustache. I didn't see him further down. I only saw him down to his waist. He had a camouflage uniform with a pattern of light and dark green.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: He stood there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He stood there at the entrance into Hasim Ahmic's and Fahrudin's yard. He was at the fence, at the very entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you know that Hasim Ahmic, at that time, was coming to collect his clothes in his home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother saw Hasim Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: No, no, not your mother. What did you see? Did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that he stood there, but in Zenica, in the statement you gave on February 2, 1998, you said that he walked up and that he was 15 metres away. Today you said 20 metres away, but in the first statement in '97, you said that he was 30 metres away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it's not that much of a difference. I mean, 15, 20 to 30 metres, it's not, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Well, this is a quantitative difference, I mean, 30 metres compared to 15 metres, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously, I could see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Whose houses are next to Drago Josipovic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whose houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Next to Drago Josipovic, there is his mother's house, Luca's house. His mother's name is Luca. Then Hasim Ahmic's house, Fahran Ahmic's house. On the left-hand side, left of his house when we look at it from up here, is his cousin's house, Jozo's house, Vlado Santic's house, and on the other side, a bit further up, is Sukrita's house. There is Muzafer's (phoen) house, also, his brother-in-law's house. All of these are, sort of, together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did you do your military service in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In 1989, I did my military service in the former army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did Drago Josipovic and Slavica come to see you off when you went to the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: No? Not that they called on you, but did they come to see you off then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did Karahodza tell you whether there was someone else with him in Ogrjev, within the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone was with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did he tell you about someone else being a watchman there and then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that Jukic from Nadioci was there. I don't know what his first name is. I think that he was also a watchman with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said you think. Don't tell me what you think. Tell me what you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Jukic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How do you know that Jukic was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know him. I know that he worked in Ogrjev first, at Poculica, and then he was transferred to here, to work with Aladin. One night, it was Aladin, and one night, it was this other man, Jukic, whose shift it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: That day, was anybody else on duty, apart from Karahodza? Did Karahodza tell you anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether he told you anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: If you were in a state of shock when you watched this, was your eyesight dimmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. When I watched what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said that you were in shock.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in shock when I walked into the APC, when the APC came to Nova Bila, Dolac, approximately, I think. I don't know. I was somewhere around Nova Bila and Dolac because I know that we quickly reached Travnik, the hospital. My wife and my mother told me about this, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: When you were in shock; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you, sometime between Nova Bila and Dolac, I was in a state of shock.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How did you feel when you were waiting for the APC, because in the first statement you said that you were already in a state of shock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is only normal. Everybody was afraid. I was afraid. Everybody was afraid because we were awaiting death, because they had rifles and we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Who are you referring to when you say "they had rifles"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the HVO, because they are the only ones who had rifles in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because I was afraid for my mother, my wife. If I were alone, I could have had an opportunity. I mean, my own life didn't matter to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Could you please answer the following question: You said in your first statement that you were in a state of shock. When did you go into a state of shock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I got into a state of shock.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: How did you feel when you were waiting for the APCs to come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fear prevailed, of course, naturally. It's a kind of shock, fear. I think fear is a kind of shock. You feel lost, that you can't see anything in front of your eyes, that your eyesight is dimmed when you're afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You also said that Aladin Karahodza told you something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Aladin?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes, Aladin. What did he tell you, that Drago Josipovic allegedly told him something or threatened him or what? I'll remind you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You don't have to remind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I have to remind you. You said what, that he would sweeten things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And, you know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sweeten and become colder, it's more or less the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: The transcript. Your Honour, there's no transcript on our screen, and it has been that way for the last few minutes. I think there's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: You're right. I wonder whether Counsel Susak would be so kind as to wait a few seconds before asking his next question so we can have the translation, because it is too quick and probably the interpreters cannot cope with so many quick questions and answers. I see the transcript is now coming back. Counsel Susak, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: However, you made a different statement to the investigator, and that is on 10th of May this year, and both are under quotation marks, and there you said that Drago said to Aladin, "Sugar comes at the end." That is quite different. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sugar comes at the end? I don't know. I said he would sweeten things with him or get colder. I mean, doesn't it mean the same thing? That's the way it is; isn't it? Because you always have to sweeten your coffee, right? If you like sweet coffee.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Well, you're very clever, aren't you? Like you were with the investigator in Zenica. You know what you said under quotation marks, both one and the other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said I'm saying now too. I could write a book on all the things that we lived through and how we went through all of this. Everything that I said is true. A word or two that are --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Was there any glass in the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Ogrjev you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Yes. How come Aladin didn't previously break the glass on the windows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I imagine he saw this army, these soldiers, and he didn't dare go out because they were the only ones who walked, not us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what you think but what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you what he told me, that Drago Josipovic, in the morning, around 2.00 a.m. --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You don't have to repeat all of that. Just did he tell you that there were glass windows or did you see glass windows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw this glass on the lower side, but I didn't see a door. I only saw him in front of the door, standing in front of the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: And in other places? Are there any windows on this particular facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the lower side, and there is a door, and he was there at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: From the aerial photograph you could see that there are several windows and on the ground floor too.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but he didn't dare go out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: You said today that he waved with his hand. Could you explain these circumstances, how Aladin waved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was standing and waving like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Did he put his hand out of the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was standing in front of the door, in front of this little house, when he saw us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: So as far as I could understand, the warehouse wasn't closed or locked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: All right. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Puliselic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Witness Z, my name is Petar Puliselic. I'm an attorney, Defence counsel, and I would like to put a few questions to you. At the beginning of your statement today, you spoke of events from the 20th of October, 1992. In your opinion, what was it that led to this conflict? Could you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 19th of October, orders were received to open a checkpoint to prevent the forces from going to Novi Travnik. Naturally, that is exactly what we did. We established this checkpoint on the 19th, in the evening -- it was dusk rather -- in order to prevent a large concentration of the Croatian Defence Council. And they started from Poculica, Kiseljak, Busovaca towards Novi Travnik. And since the fighting had already broken out in Novi Travnik --

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said that you received orders. Could you tell us more accurately who did you receive these orders from to set up this roadblock, this checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, because we belonged to the headquarters of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were conflicts in Jajce, and that the HVO was defending Jajce from the Serbs and that Jajce was about to fall? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was fighting going on in Jajce, but allegedly we also knew that the HVO had set out on Novi Travnik rather than Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Does one reach Jajce through Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: What do you mean no? How can you reach Jajce? What is the closest way from Busovaca to Jajce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Travnik Common.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Jajce fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only afterwards. Since I was in the village there in Ahmici, only when we started walking and when I reported to the headquarters of Territorial Defence in Stari Vitez, that is when I found out about the fall of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Who else was there apart from you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Were all of them in uniform, and did they all have weapons? What kind of weapons did they have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Since we belonged to the Territorial Defence headquarters, to the Military Police, we were at this checkpoint. I happened to be at home --

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, camouflage uniforms. Can I just explain this? Not all of us had camouflage uniforms. We would leave them there. We would wear civilian clothes when we went to work, to the headquarters of Territorial Defence, and then when we would go home we would take off these uniforms because we didn't have too many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: How many people were there around the roadblock? I'm not saying at the roadblock itself, but in the vicinity. Were there any trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a dugout improvised, without a roof. I don't know exactly how many people were there, because I was there until 3.00 and then I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: There was shooting, you said. How long did this shooting last approximately? You said that it started when, early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning I woke up around 4.30, because I went towards the mosque of Hadzija Ahmic. I went to that part of the village, and I managed to get to Nedzib Ahmic's house, then a shell was fired from the direction of Zume, and it hit the top of the minaret, and that is when shooting broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how long all of this lasted, this shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then the shooting went on for a short while and then it subsided. Ten, eleven -- I don't know. Perhaps until 12.00 all of this went on, this very strong shooting. They were shooting from all the weapons they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: All right. But here the roadblock also and around it, did they shoot there too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one was at the roadblock any longer, because I was there until 3:00 and they had withdrawn in the morning when they heard this, because there was a fog that morning, and they managed to pull out towards this part of the village called Krcevine, up there. So they left this roadblock.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: And what did they set up there, a frontline or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, naturally. When someone is shooting at you, you have to defend yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: All right. So there was shooting both ways; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. I don't know. Perhaps three or four bullets were fired only from the place where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: In that conflict, did Croats from Ahmici take part in that conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats from Ahmici? I didn't see any of them then. I didn't see any of them that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did Croats from Ahmici ask the Muslim population to come back to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that really.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: The population came back, you know that; don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Only eight days later I went back to the village, to my own house, to see what was going on with my house, because in the lower part there weren't any civilians. Only up there in Zume. You know, those were the only civilians that were there, but not down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But everything was all right with your house; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was drilled with bullets. If my father was not there, it would have burned down, because he spent the night there and there were tracer bullets that were fired at the house. He was there all day with neighbours and with my mother, and he was crawling on his hands and knees, and he was collecting bullets and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Dragan Papic too, and you said that you saw him once with a sniper up there by the school, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: And also toward the Kupreskic houses, that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you see what kind of a sniper this was, what kind of a weapon this was? Was it for hunting, was it a military sniper? What kind of sniper was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a military sniper. A military sniper with a sight, an optical sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: How come you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How could I not know. In the former army we saw different weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: What is the difference between a military sniper and a hunting sniper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their functions are the same, but the other one is bigger and heavier. The hunting one is lighter, and its range is shorter than that of a military one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: All right. But according to form when you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The military sniper is more massive than the hunting one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said he wore a black uniform and that it was too short for him, too small or something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The sleeves were too short, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did this uniform have some insignia on it? What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a cap with a U on it. He had this cap on the epaulet, on his shoulder, and he didn't have any insignia but the cap had a U on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You did not mention the cap until now. During the examination by the Prosecutor, on previous occasions you didn't mention it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I imagine I admitted it, because he was in that uniform non-stop. From the first conflict to the second conflict he was in that black uniform non-stop, and we, the Bosniaks, know what a black uniform means.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's an Ustashe uniform. During the former war, our parents and grandparents remembered what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do Ustashes wear only that kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who was a Ustashe wore that kind of uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: All Ustashe wore such uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Darko Kraljevic and his group, they wore those uniforms in Vitez. Not all of them. The HOS also wore that uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I wanted to say that the Ustashe army did not have such uniforms.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Some had camouflage uniforms, others this black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: And I'm talking about Ustashe army in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You spoke about shooting on the 16th of April, how it started, and I think you said that you were on duty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I was protecting my house in the night during the 15th and the 16th. It wasn't a sort of watch, it was just looking out for the safety of our houses. I went to sleep at 2.00, but whether Ekrem Imsirevic waited until morning, I don't know. I went to sleep at 2.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you take off your uniform when you went to bed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The situation was very tense, you understand me. As I said, up until the 15th there was a great deal of tension and silence. There will never be silence like that again. It was deadly silence. You just couldn't -- it was so tense that you found it very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: And then you took your top off?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just took my jacket off.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Afterwards when you got up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the 16th, when I saw that the soldiers were in my yard and were running across it, I just said to my mother, "Well, they're already in our yard."

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: And then you took off this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I threw it away into the cupboard, and I placed the rifle in the cupboard, and my vest as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: In the statement to the investigators of the 10th of March, 1998, you state that from your house you heard the sound of anti-aircraft weapons from the vicinity of Ivo and Mario Papic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the forest I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said that you heard it, and now you say that you saw that there was shooting from the PAT, the automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw tracer bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Where did you see those tracer bullets? Did you see them up in the air or where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I saw them ricocheting from the houses, the walls of the houses. And from Rovna I saw them targeting the Ahmici houses. Along the asphalt road, the ammunition was riveted from the ground and became lodged in the surrounding walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But how did you conclude that this ammunition was coming from the anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said that I'd already been in the army and been at the frontline towards the Serbs in Visoko, and that we had encountered weapons of this kind. We knew how the weapons fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But you did not see the PAT, the semi-automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see the PAT, but I saw it shooting. It is an anti-aircraft gun.
