utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: So you saw these shells in the air; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. From the direction of the wood, going down towards the lower part of the mosque, the lower part of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you see the PAT, the anti-aircraft gun?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but I saw the ammunition firing from the wood, and these tracer bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said in your statement to the investigator that it was a PAT -- a 40-millimetre PAT anti-aircraft gun.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was approximately 40 millimetres, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Is that quite certain? Are you sure that it was that type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, we had already encountered guns of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: I know that you'd already encountered them, but how can you determine this on the basis of the tracer bullets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I said that it was -- that I thought it was a 40-millimetre anti-aircraft gun know as PAT.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what I wanted to hear, because you say you saw these anti-aircraft guns, whereas to the investigator you said you had just heard them. You mention, furthermore, the wood, a wood. You said that it was -- it belonged to Dragan and Ivo Papic. Do you know who the owner of the wood is and whether Dragan Papic is the owner of any part of the wood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, his father is the owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: His father then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is their property. It did not belong to me, it wasn't mine. They were there and it was theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the owners of the wood are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that it belonged to Dragan Papic and his father, and Marija, that they had part of the wood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the largest part of the wood belonged to Ante Papic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the other part of the forest belonged to Gavro Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they used the wood as if it were their own. They walked around it, they stayed there, and at the first instance the army was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a large portion of the wood belonged to Simo Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that a very small part of the wood, in fact, belonged to Ivo and Marija Papic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know that they did have a wood there. I said it was theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You said that you were on good terms, you and your family, with the Papic family, Ivo and Dragan Papic's family, and you, I think, said that you visited each other.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we did visit each other. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You even knew who lived in the house, in which part of the house, where the individual members of the family slept. How many members did the Papic family have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know where they slept, but I did go into their property. I did not go into their bedrooms, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that to the investigator, you knew exactly who was on the ground floor level and who was on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When Dragan Papic married, he lived on the first floor of the house with his wife, and we went there for a house warming party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he married? When did Dragan Papic marry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was in 1991, I think. 1990 or '91. I don't quite remember. Between 1990 and 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But you told the investigator that in the upper part of the house Ivo Papic and his wife lived, and that is why I'm asking of these details?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they lived in the same house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: But you said that they were on the first floor. Now you say that Dragan lived on the first floor, but never mind. Can you tell us, please -- you, of course, know where the Lasva River lies. Can you tell us how far the river is from the road, the main road passing through Ahmici? Can you show us on the map? Would you indicate to the Court, using a pointer, where the Lasva River lies? Yes, it's course. Would you show the course of the river to the end? On the other side as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This way. It flows this way (indicating). This is the bridge for Donja Rovna, that bridge (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: You indicated the bridge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: What is it called? What is the bridge called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the bridge for Donja Rovna, lower Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Is it called Radak's bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: So the road led across the bridge towards lower Rovna. Did a road exist before the war? Did another road exist? As far as I can see, there was another road along the Lasva River. Did the road exist before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean along the Lasva River?

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Were they fields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was the old railway line.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: No, across the bridge. The other side of the bridge when you cross the Lasva River. There is a white line on the map. When you cross over the bridge to the other side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, and it reads towards Rovna.

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: Yes, but along the river there is a parallel white line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a footpath. Not a road, a footpath. I passed there once because it was a footpath, as I say. Otherwise we went to the Lasva River to bathe. But I didn't cross over very often, I just crossed over once, and I took this footpath and went towards Rasko Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions. Counsel Slokovic-Glumac. Counsel Susak, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. SUSAK
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the translation I found that the last statement was given by the witness on the 10th of May, 1998. He made the statement on the 10th of March, 1998. There was an error there. One other point, Mr. President. I would like to propose that the statements given by this witness on the 16th and 17th of November, 1997, as well as on the 2nd of February, 1998, and the statement of the 3rd of March, 1999 (sic) be tendered into evidence, because they are all different and they differ in relation to what the witness said today, and this is vital evidence, I feel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I wonder whether the Prosecution is against?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as these three statements are concerned, there is no problem. I'm sure that the Judges will be able to make up their mind on the pretended -- the alleged differences that are to be found in these statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So they are admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. The statements will be marked D3/5, D4/5 and D5/5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Slokovic-Glumac?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Good day to you. I'm going to ask you something with regard to the barricade -- or it was not, in fact, a barricade but a checkpoint, let us say, at the entrance to Ahmici. You mentioned it, that it was set up after the return from Upper Ahmici or Vrhovine, and that it was set up at the entrance to Ahmici. You spoke about the checkpoint when you mentioned the three names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That checkpoint was set up on the day after in October when the conflict had already broken out, on the first day, on the 20th of October. On the 21st of October the checkpoint was set up. We had withdrawn to the upper part of Ahmici, and the checkpoint was there from the 21st until we returned. I can give you an example.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one moment. I'm first going to refer to what you said in your statement, and then we'll see later on. So you came to the checkpoint when you returned to Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went from -- I left my house for the first day after eight days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you left on the 20th of October to Upper Ahmici. You had escaped there and you returned when?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 28th. And then I went to my house.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You were appointed to that checkpoint to take up your duties there. Who gave you orders to go to the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as the first conflict had already broken out, we had been given instructions to protect the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who told you to man the checkpoint? At what level was an agreement reached that you should guard the checkpoint together with the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably from the Territorial Defence headquarters in Vitez, as I was in the Military Police already, and as I was already working on the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: That means that from the Territorial Defence headquarters in Vitez, an order was issued that, together with the Croats, you should man the checkpoint, is that correct, at the entrance to the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I was wearing civilian clothing. I was not wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: I'm not asking what you were wearing, I just want to clarify how you came to man the checkpoint. Very well then. At the checkpoint, there was you and there were the Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was the checkpoint a lasting checkpoint? That is to say, how long was it maintained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for about 10 to 12 days, not longer than that. I did not see the checkpoint after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So that means that the checkpoint existed for about 10 days, and it was a combined checkpoint, a joint checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a joint checkpoint for eight days, and after eight -- they were alone for the first eight days, up to the eighth day.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Now, I'm asking you something else. I am talking about the fact that you said that a decision had been made to man the checkpoint with combined forces, and you said that this decision was made at a higher level. You don't know exactly at what level, but that it was decided to set up a checkpoint at the entrance to Ahmici; is that correct? Therefore, I'm now asking you after that time, when you, together with the Croats, manned the checkpoint, how long did that last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It lasted two or three days, not longer. Two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And was the checkpoint disbanded afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So neither the Croats nor the Bosnians manned the checkpoint at the entrance to Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At the checkpoint, the checkpoint was envisaged to be manned jointly by the Croats and Bosnians. Was there any mention of having two by two, or what was the arrangement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I was assigned to the checkpoint myself, alone. I was the only individual there. I was there for about two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you were the only person to return down there at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not return, I went to see my house. That is when everything started, the gradual return.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But in this gradual return, it was decided to man the checkpoint together at the entrance to the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether you had a rifle at that time with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was at the checkpoint, no. I was just wearing civilian clothes and had my hands in my pockets, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the checkpoint was an improvised checkpoint. There were no mines or other devices. It was not an actual barricade, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Was there a physical boundary or were there only people there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, for the first eight days, there was a physical obstacle, a barrier, but they wouldn't let any Muslims there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: How do you know they didn't give any Muslims a chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, my uncle lives in Vitez, and he came to see what was happening to us, and he went towards the upper village, and Dragan Papic stopped him and did not allow him to pass into the upper village to see what had happened to us, whether we were alive or not. He can confirm this any time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: At that time, where were you, in Vrhovine or in Upper Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in Upper Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was the majority of the population who had escaped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them were at Vrhovine and the rest were in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, whether, in the first conflict, some Croatian property -- was Croatian property burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You didn't see that any Croatian sheds had been set fire to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that. All I know is that 13 of our sheds and 5 houses were burnt. My shed was burnt; my car was burnt. They killed two cows. When my mother let the cows go off on their own, the cows were killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something more about the checkpoint and the first conflict. Do you recall whether the first people manning the checkpoint happened to stop a vehicle belonging to the Croatian Regional Police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regional police, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civilian police, yes, they did, because there was an accident, and one of my relatives, Sulejman Ahmic, was doing a shift and somebody else. I don't know his name. There was an accident at the entrance to Nadioci. There was a car accident and somebody was killed. They took people on the spot. They went there to investigate, and they had no problems in passing when they came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So the car was stopped. It was the car belonging to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not stopped. They just asked what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, the people who were stopped, were there weapons taken from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, nobody did that while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: While you were there, yes. Was the vehicle confiscated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that you left at about 3.00 a.m. in the morning. Do you know whether anybody else's car was confiscated and weapons confiscated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. While I was there, it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Where was Sulejman Ahmic, the one that you mentioned? Where was he, at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He was not at the barricade. He worked in the civilian police force, because the civilian police force was still functioning, and the Bosnians and Serbs and Croats were together. They were a combined civilian police force. That's as far as the civilian police is concerned; whereas, the Military Police, that was already separate. The separation had already started.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who was the commander at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there was no commander there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: There was no commander, you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: For example, if you were given the order to set up a barricade, who would then decide what was to happen at the barricade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were members of the Military Police already, and we had worked together at barricades, and they assigned us to that particular barricade from the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Who gave you this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was issued by telephone. I don't know, but I was there -- as I say, I was on my way home, and they told us to set up a checkpoint there because there were strong forces moving towards Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So there were people from the reserve police force there as well, the Military Police, that is to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did the Territorial Defence from Ahmici take part in setting up the barricade and in manning the barricade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were up by Krcevine. We were at the barricade alone.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: They were in Krcevine. How were they there? They were there to protect you? They were your security?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: With rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they carried what they had.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: In the trench at the side, how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About three to four. It was a very small trench. I don't remember who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were they people from the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Civilians, you say, with rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, some people had rifles. Some didn't. There was one rifle to every three individuals, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did people from Vrhovine come and the surrounding villages? Did they come as reinforcements to help you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: -- while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What was the barricade made up of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know, sort of logs, wood, just a sort of obstacle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Were there any mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. While I was there, there were no mines. Until 3.00 a.m. in the morning, there were no mines. Whether somebody brought some mines later on, I really can't say. But while I was there, up to 3.00 a.m., there were not any.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you did not see any mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said that the checkpoint at the entrance to the village was put up after the 21st when all the Muslims left; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right, from that part. Do you know who was at that checkpoint? How did you manage to see that it was established on the 21st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it could be seen quite clearly from the upper part of Ahmici. You can see it with your very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: What is it that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We would see them go home and come there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So when it was decided for you to go back, then the decision was made for you to guard the checkpoint together; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Just one more question, and my colleagues already put this question, but I'm only interested in the following: Before the 15th, how much time did you spend at home? Did you come every day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you go to work on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came, perhaps, on the 14th or the 15th. I don't know exactly when I came. Otherwise, we could not come. We would spend four or five days up there in the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, and then we would spend about 15 days at the frontline, even up to a month. It all depended, really.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you arrived sometime on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 14th or 15th. I came to get a bit of a rest, and I hadn't been home for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: When you were on guard, you were usually in uniform; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At least I was in uniform, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You put on your uniform for guard duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I wore it anyway, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you wear a uniform all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not when I was at home. At home, I would wear civilian clothes. I could hardly wait to put on civilian clothes. We would leave our uniforms back at the headquarters, and we would go home in civilian clothes so that others could wear the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you didn't leave this one at the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I took it in a plastic bag. I came by car so I also brought my rifle in the passenger car. I hid it because they searched us at checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: So you went on guard duty in uniform; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You said who was with you, Galib Imsirevic; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did he have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: A semi-automatic rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: And his father, Ekrem Imsirevic, did he have a rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He only took a rifle, when he came around 2.00, from Galib Imsirevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: All right. Who was he with on guard duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean with whom? You mean Ekrem?

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Yes, Ekrem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ekrem stayed on, on his own.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: On his own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Did you do this every evening or how did you organise this at Krcevine, this guard duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there, so we would just walk out in front of the house. I didn't go up to Krcevine. No, I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Oh, so you didn't. You guarded the places around your own houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But you also tried to have a weapon on; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, those were the times.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that the times were such and that you remember the day before that there was great tension in the air?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: You also said that there was a strange atmosphere, that no one trusted anyone any longer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. No one would speak, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: No one would even speak, I see. Was a decision made after the people, the Bosniaks, returned to the village not even to say hello to Croats, not even to talk the Croats? Wasn't such a decision made to cool off relations completely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We did not expect our neighbours, our former neighbours, to do that kind of thing. We had trusted them and we had lived with them. They did to us what they did to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: After the first conflict, you said that this was a moral attitude of every person, not to speak to a Croat. Now you said, a few minutes ago, that the Croats around the village did not take part in the attack at all on the 20th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Croat from Vitez or from Ahmici, it's all the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Oh, so it's all the same. Who are the Croats who attacked you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All of them attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But the important thing was that they were Croats, right, the people from the village and all that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Tell me, is it possible that the Croats didn't trust the Muslims either? You said that no one trusted anyone. Is it possible that they didn't trust you either?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't trust them, and I don't know whether they trusted us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: But there was reason for you to trust one another, because you are speaking in these categories. It is all the same to you, whether it's a Croat from the village or any other Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day in the village, I didn't see anyone. I told you that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume Counsel Radovic has quite a few questions, otherwise, we could finish before lunch. Mr. Radovic, do you have many questions or just one or two?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I have many questions. I imagine that we will be able to finish with this witness before lunch, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: When you were in the headquarters of the Territorial Defence, did all members of the staff wear a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: According to what criteria? Did some people have a uniform and others not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Priority was given to people who were on the frontline against the Serbs. They got uniforms the most. The Military Police, also, who were on guard duty and went to the frontline, they received uniforms. Whoever went to the frontline against the Serbs would get uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what do you believe the staff of the Territorial Defence to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the staff was the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Who belonged to the staff? You don't have to give us the names, but tell us the number of people that belonged to the staff, according to you? Did you belong to this staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I belonged to the staff of the Military Police of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: So you were in charge --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Defence counsel is overlapping the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Those who were in the staff, that is to say, those who were in the leadership, did they all have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Now I'm asking you, once again, according to what criterion, and it is officers who belong to a staff, according to what criterion did they have uniforms or did they not have uniforms? Do you know anyone who did not have a uniform? Again, you don't have to mention names. If you remember, then we're going to ask for a closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you know, they went through town every day. When they would go to the frontline, they would wear a uniform, but while they were there in town, they didn't have to wear a uniform. Some of them, perhaps, did have uniforms and others did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we have a closed session for awhile so that we could hear who did have uniforms and who did not have uniforms or shall we, perhaps, continue this after lunch? Would that be better, after all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: After lunch, yes. We will adjourn now until 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m. 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)
